canonical_statement: The review objective was to determine the effects of UFH or LMWH compared with placebo or untreated control for non-ST elevation acute coronary syndromes.
Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults with unstable angina or NSTEMI requiring treatment within 72 hours of the last chest-pain episode.

population.label: Adults with NSTEACS requiring treatment within 72 hours
inclusion_criteria: Treatment required within 72 hours of last chest-pain episode

canonical_statement: The 2014 update searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL and LILACS through 15 January 2014 without language restrictions.
Study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment used independent review by two authors with consensus resolution of disagreements.
Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool across seven domains and presented in summary and graph form.

Pooled dichotomous outcomes were summarized as risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals; random-effects models were used when more than five trials were pooled, otherwise fixed-effect models were used when appropriate, and heterogeneity was quantified with I-squared.
The review used GRADE to assess the body of evidence for risk of bias, directness, inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias.
Eight randomized trials with 3118 participants were included; average age was 62 years, approximately 75% were male, and 52% were eligible to receive LMWH while 48% were eligible to receive UFH.

canonical_statement: A planned subgroup analysis comparing unstable angina with NSTEMI could not be performed because subgroup data were unavailable from the included studies.
Only one included study was assessed as low risk of bias overall; several trials had unclear allocation methods and multiple trials had high-risk blinding or other-bias domains.
GRADE classified the evidence as low quality for all clinically important outcomes, and the review concluded that the methodological quality of the trials was far from optimal.
The evidence came from older trials conducted before P2Y12 receptor blockers were widely used, limiting applicability to contemporary dual-antiplatelet-treated NSTEACS populations.
Minor bleeding was reported in only three studies and thrombocytopenia in only two, and side effects were poorly reported in most included studies.
The funnel plot suggested possible publication bias, but the number of studies was insufficient for rigorous funnel-plot assessment.
The mortality analysis was underpowered for modest treatment effects because death occurred in only about 1% to 2% of participants.

The review authors concluded that heparin reduced myocardial infarction but not mortality, while increasing minor bleeding; revascularization, recurrent angina, and thrombocytopenia were similar to control.
The authors supported early heparin treatment for NSTEACS but stated that the small number of studies prevented recommendation of a particular dosing regimen.
The authors cautioned that indirect comparisons suggesting LMWH may be more effective than UFH were unreliable and potentially misleading.
The review listed internal institutional support and external support from the Canada Institute of Health Research.
The authors declared no known conflicts of interest.
In 2021 the review was declared stable because heparin had become standard care for acute coronary syndromes and new placebo-controlled trials meeting the eligibility criteria were not expected.
